key_insight: RGR moves stochastic gradient estimation to Euclidean space before retracting to the Stiefel manifold, eliminating vector transport and enabling adaptive, horizon-free optimization with strong complexity guarantees.
engineering_relevance: This gives machine learning and deep learning practitioners a more practical way to train orthogonality-constrained models such as PCA, matrix completion, and orthogonal CNNs without tuning steps from unknown smoothness or training horizon.
method: RGR computes recursive gradient estimators in Euclidean space, then maps them to the tangent space via retraction.
RGR-SPIDER is designed for finite-sum problems with adaptive, Lipschitz-free and horizon-free stepsizes.
RGR-SRM and RGR-EMA target online stochastic settings with mini-batch and horizon-free parameter choices.
evidence_signal: The paper reports theoretical convergence rates and experiments on PCA, low-rank matrix completion, and orthogonal convolutional neural networks, where RGR variants converge faster than tangent-space recursive methods.
watch_item: Performance depends on manifold retraction quality and careful implementation of adaptive estimator updates, so empirical gains may vary across Stiefel problems and batch-noise regimes.
paper_title: Recursive Gradient Retraction Methods for Stochastic Nonconvex Optimization on Stiefel Manifolds
